books.section: Topic 4.11 An Age of Reform, B. Debating the Future of Slavery in America

primary_sources: Frederick Douglass, Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, 1845

stimulus.text: "The more I read, the more I was led to abhor and detest my enslavers. I could regard them in no other light than a band of successful robbers, who had left their homes, and gone to Africa, and stolen us from our homes, and in a strange land reduced us to slavery." — Frederick Douglass, Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, 1845
stimulus.source_note: Verbatim public-domain quotation from Frederick Douglass, Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass (Boston: Anti-Slavery Office, 1845), Chapter VII. Wording checked against the Project Gutenberg text and the UNC Documenting the American South edition.

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim public-domain quotation from Douglass, Narrative (1845)
stem: The passage's publication in 1845 mattered to abolitionism mainly because

options.text: it proved the Liberator's editors wrong about slavery's nature
options.misconception: Douglass and Garrison were allies; the Narrative supported the Liberator, not refuted it.

options.text: a formerly enslaved man's testimony gave evidence no white writer could
it called for the colonization of freed people in Liberia
options.misconception: Douglass opposed colonization; he demanded rights in America, not removal.

options.text: it defended gradual emancipation over immediate abolition
options.misconception: Douglass demanded freedom now; his life story argues for immediatism, not delay.

rationales.A: Douglass spoke at abolitionist meetings and wrote for the movement. His Narrative strengthened Garrison's paper, it did not prove it wrong.
rationales.B: A white writer could argue against slavery, but only a formerly enslaved person could testify from inside it. Douglass's own story was evidence of a new kind.
rationales.C: Douglass called colonization a plan that accommodated slavery. His book argues for freedom and equality in the United States.
rationales.D: Douglass escaped slavery and demanded its immediate end. Nothing in the Narrative asks the nation to wait.
rationales.general:
1. Ask who is speaking. A man who lived slavery writes his own life, in his own words.
2. Ask what only he can give. No white abolitionist could testify from inside the slave's experience.
3. Name the value. His testimony turned argument into evidence.
Background: Douglass escaped from slavery in 1838 and became the most famous Black abolitionist speaker in America.
Remember: testimony beats argument when the question is what something felt like — ask who lived it.
